questions.q: Which statement most precisely matches this lesson's definition of least privilege?
options: Grant users a generous safety margin above what they currently need, to avoid future support tickets
Grant a user, process, or integration exactly the access needed to do its job, no more
Grant every user the System Administrator profile and remove permissions later if problems arise
Grant access based on seniority rather than job function
questions.explain: Least privilege means exactly the access needed and no more -- any extra access granted "to be safe" or "to save time later" is unused risk, not a harmless margin.

questions.q: In Salesforce's access model, what is the main structural difference between a profile and a permission set?
options: A profile is additive and assigned to individuals; a permission set sets the shared baseline for everyone with that profile
There is no structural difference -- they grant identical kinds of access
A profile sets the shared baseline access for everyone assigned it; a permission set grants additional access on top of that baseline to specific users who need it
Permission sets can only restrict access, never grant it
questions.explain: Profiles set the baseline shared by every assigned user; permission sets are additive and assignable to individuals, which is what lets an architect grant a narrow extra capability to only the people who actually need it.

questions.q: Why does this lesson treat an org full of users with unneeded "Modify All Data" access as a real defect rather than a harmless convenience?
options: Because Salesforce bills extra for every user with that permission
Because it has no actual security implication and is only a cosmetic issue
Because "Modify All Data" is a deprecated permission that no longer functions
Because unused permissions are unmanaged risk sitting in the org, waiting for a credential compromise or a mistaken action to turn into real damage
questions.explain: Over-permissioning isn't neutral -- every unneeded permission is unused risk that a phished credential, stolen device, or honest mistake can turn into real harm, which is why an architect treats it the same way a code reviewer treats dead code: as a finding.

questions.q: What does this lesson say is the correct design direction for building least privilege, as opposed to the common shortcut?
options: Start from the minimum baseline and add specific, justified permission sets only where a real need exists
Start from a broad admin-level grant and remove unneeded permissions later on an as-needed basis
Grant access based on whichever profile is fastest to clone, regardless of fit
Skip profiles entirely and assign every permission through permission sets only
questions.explain: The lesson argues design should run from nothing upward -- minimum baseline plus justified additions -- because in practice, the "grant broad access and remove it later" shortcut rarely gets the removal step done on schedule, if ever.

questions.q: What does a "muting permission set" let an architect do, per this lesson?
options: Permanently delete a permission set from the org
Grant a permission set group's permissions to a user while explicitly removing one or two specific permissions from within that group for a subset of users
Hide a permission set from the Setup UI without changing its effect
Automatically rotate which users are assigned a permission set each month
questions.explain: A muting permission set, used within a permission set group, narrows access back down for specific users by explicitly removing select permissions from an otherwise-shared group, without having to rebuild the whole group.
